title: Can Mandated Political Representation Increase Policy Influence for Disadvantaged Minorities? Theory and Evidence from India
research_question: Does mandating political representation for historically disadvantaged groups translate into greater policy influence for those groups, specifically affecting the level and composition of redistributive public spending? Do legislators' group identities shape policy outcomes once electoral accountability and party competition are taken into account?
data_description: The analysis uses a state-level panel covering the 16 major Indian states (Punjab and Haryana entering in 1965) over 1960-1992, with targeted welfare spending variables available for 1974-1992. Policy outcomes include real per capita total state expenditure, share of state budget on education, passage of land reform acts, share of budget devoted to scheduled caste and scheduled tribe welfare programs, and the share of state government jobs reserved for these groups. Key explanatory variables are the proportion of state legislative jurisdictions reserved for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes and the corresponding population shares, drawn from decennial censuses (interpolated for inter-census years). Additional controls include real per capita state income, population density, age distribution, Gini coefficients from National Sample Surveys, a political Herfindahl index, swing-group indicators, and an election-year dummy. Sources include Election Commission reports, Reserve Bank of India publications, the Ministry of Welfare, and the Census of India.
institutional_context: The Indian Constitution mandates that a fixed share of state legislative jurisdictions be set aside for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes—historically disadvantaged groups comprising roughly 16% and 8% of the population. In reserved jurisdictions, only members of the designated group may stand for election, while the entire electorate votes, so the mandate alters legislator identity without changing voter identity. The share of reserved jurisdictions in each state must mirror the group's population share according to the most recent census, and revisions occur only when fresh census estimates arrive and are implemented by the national Election Commission and Delimitation Commission. Because state elections occur in different years and the share of reserved seats adjusts to population changes only with a lag, within-state variation in the extent of reservation arises from institutional rather than contemporaneous political processes. Indian states have substantial autonomy over redistributive policies, including welfare programs and job quotas targeted at these groups.

main_estimate.unit: fraction of state budget increase in SC-targeted welfare spending per additional SC reserved seat
main_estimate.interpretation: One additional reserved legislative seat for Scheduled Castes increases state government spending on SC welfare programs by approximately 1.5% of the total state budget

secondary_estimate.unit: fraction of state budget increase in ST-targeted spending per additional ST reserved seat
secondary_estimate.interpretation: Similarly, one additional reserved seat for Scheduled Tribes increases targeted tribal welfare spending by approximately 2% of state budget

public_sources: Indian Census (population by caste/tribe — available from Office of Registrar General)
Election Commission of India (assembly election results and reservation data — public)
Reserve Bank of India (state finance data — public)
data_availability.proxy_strategy: Most data is available from Indian government sources. Census data, election results, and state finance data are public. Replication data available from the author.
data_availability.replicability: medium — Indian government data is public but can be difficult to compile; replication data available from author
data_availability.replication_tier: full (Indian Census + Election Commission + RBI state finances — all public; replication data available)
data_availability.data_limitations: State-level analysis has only 16 major states, limiting degrees of freedom. Census enumeration of SC/ST populations may be influenced by political considerations. Multiple rounding thresholds within each state create many potential discontinuities but each with limited local sample. State budget data quality varies across states and time periods.
public_data_sources_detail: Census of India (SC/ST population shares — public from censusindia.gov.in)
Election Commission of India (reservation data and results — public)
RBI (state government finance data — public from rbi.org.in)

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Regression discontinuity design — running variable is minority (SC/ST) population share in the state; the step function mapping population share to number of reserved seats creates multiple discontinuities (at each rounding threshold); an additional reserved seat is the treatment; redistributive policy is the outcome

key_variables.treatment: one additional reserved seat for SC or ST in the state legislative assembly (determined by rounding of population share × total seats)
key_variables.control: states with one fewer reserved seat (just below the rounding threshold)
key_variables.outcome: state government spending on SC/ST welfare, job reservation (quota) implementation, land reform policies, minority public sector employment

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Mandated minority representation significantly increases redistributive policy favoring the represented group. One additional reserved seat for Scheduled Castes increases state spending on SC welfare programs and strengthens implementation of job reservation (quota) policies. Similarly, additional ST seats increase spending on tribal welfare. The effects are concentrated in policy domains most salient to the minority group (welfare spending, job quotas) rather than general public goods.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: One additional SC reserved seat increases SC-targeted welfare spending by approximately 1-2% of total state budget; one additional ST seat increases ST welfare spending by a similar magnitude
key_robustness: Separate analysis for SC and ST reservations
Controlling for state-level economic and demographic characteristics
Different polynomial specifications in population share
Placebo: reservation does not affect policies not targeted at the reserved group
State fixed effects to absorb time-invariant state characteristics

identification_strategy_detail.method: RDD exploiting the step function mapping minority population share to number of reserved assembly seats; the rounding at each integer threshold creates discontinuities in representation
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: One additional reserved legislative seat (discrete jump from the step function at rounding thresholds)
identification_strategy_detail.event_window: Policy outcomes measured during the legislative term following reapportionment
identification_strategy_detail.estimation_window: States near each rounding threshold (bandwidth in population share)
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Near the rounding thresholds, the exact minority population share is as-if random with respect to state characteristics that affect redistributive policy. Small differences in enumerated population (driven by Census enumeration quality) determine whether a state gets one more or one fewer reserved seat.

key_magnitudes.sc_welfare_spending: One additional SC reserved seat increases SC-targeted spending by approximately 1-2% of total state budget
key_magnitudes.job_quota: Stronger implementation of SC/ST job reservation policies in public sector
key_magnitudes.general_spending: No significant effect on non-targeted spending (placebo: reservation affects only targeted policies)
key_magnitudes.st_effect: ST reservation effects are similar in magnitude to SC effects

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: The step function creates multiple thresholds, providing several sources of identifying variation within each state over time. Pre-treatment state characteristics (GDP, urbanization, education) are smooth through the thresholds, supporting the RDD validity. The placebo result (no effect on non-targeted policies) is important: it confirms that the effect operates through targeted representation rather than general state capacity. Panel variation from Census-based reapportionments provides within-state identification.
